analysis.one_liner: Tightens EPA safety reviews of pesticides in food and raises training, recordkeeping, and penalty requirements for pesticide makers and applicators.
analysis.headline: The bill never reached a House floor vote: after hearings and a subcommittee approved an amended version in May 1992, it sat in the full committees until the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would overhaul how the EPA regulates pesticides. It would require the EPA to reevaluate the legal residue limits for pesticides on food whenever it has information about dietary risk, set a 'negligible risk' public-health standard for those limits, shift the legal burden onto pesticide companies that contest EPA safety orders, require periodic updated safety data from registrants, charge fees for reviews, toughen training and certification for people applying pesticides, and raise civil and criminal penalties, including new penalties for knowingly endangering people. It would also speed approval of lower-risk pesticide alternatives and support minor-use registrations that keep niche crop tools available.
analysis.who_benefits: Food consumers, who would get tighter, regularly re-evaluated residue limits on fruits, vegetables, meat, poultry, and eggs; farmworkers and rural residents, who would get better-trained applicators, pesticide-poisoning detection training, and stronger enforcement; and the public generally, through faster cancellation of pesticides found to pose unreasonable risks.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the EPA Administrator, whenever the agency has information on the dietary risk of a pesticide ingredient, to reassess the associated food-residue tolerances and take administrative action based on the findings.

Sets a public-health standard under which a pesticide residue tolerance protects the public only if the dietary risk is no greater than 'negligible,' with defined risk thresholds, and requires modification or revocation of tolerances set above that level.
Shifts the burden of persuasion in EPA proceedings to suspend, cancel, or restrict a pesticide onto the party contesting the agency's order, rather than the agency having to prove its case.

Requires pesticide applicators to be certified or supervised by certified applicators, undergo refresher training and recertification at least every five years, and receive training in detecting pesticide poisoning and emergency treatment.

Raises civil penalties to as much as $25,000 per violation (and $50,000 for repeat violations) for companies and creates new criminal 'knowing endangerment' penalties of up to $250,000 and 15 years for individuals, or up to $1,000,000 for companies.

Directs the EPA to prioritize review of registration applications for pesticide ingredients that appear significantly lower-risk than existing ones, and requires annual reports on speeding registration of biological alternatives.

analysis.who_pays: Pesticide manufacturers (registrants) would bear new costs: updated registration data on 10-year cycles, fees for periodic registration reviews and tolerance functions, the burden of proof in contesting EPA orders, and exposure to cancellation of registrations and much larger penalties. Pesticide dealers would have to keep sales records for three years, and commercial applicators would face training and recertification costs. Some compliance costs could be passed on to farmers and food prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts state and local pesticide-residue limits: states could not enforce any residue limit unless it is identical to the federal tolerance, though the EPA could approve more stringent state limits warranted by special local circumstances.

It allows continued sale and use of existing stocks of pesticides whose registrations have been suspended or canceled, at the Administrator's discretion, which delays removal of risky products from the market.

The compliance burden is real: registrants must refresh registration data on 10-year cycles and pay review fees, and those costs would likely be passed through to farmers and consumers; small farmers and private applicators face new certification and training requirements, though their penalties are capped lower ($1,000 per offense).

The bill builds in extensive procedural consultation with the Secretary of Agriculture and economic impact analyses of actions on food prices and the agricultural economy, which critics of the pesticide process at the time viewed as openings for delay of health-based restrictions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core public-health gains are real: regularly re-evaluated residue limits under a negligible-risk standard, the burden of proof shifted onto companies fighting EPA safety orders, trained and recertified applicators, and penalties large enough to matter to large companies. The costs fall mostly on pesticide registrants, which is the point of the bill, though some would flow to farmers and food prices. The genuine weaknesses are preemption of stricter state residue standards (softened by an EPA waiver process) and permission to sell off existing stocks of suspended or canceled pesticides. On balance it is a strengthening of consumer and worker protections with conventional regulatory costs, not a badly designed bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in November 1991 and sent jointly to the Agriculture and Energy and Commerce Committees; subcommittees held hearings, one subcommittee approved an amended version and sent it to the full Agriculture Committee in May 1992, and the full committees never acted before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Charlie Rose introduced the bill on November 7, 1991, and it was referred jointly to the House Agriculture Committee and the House Energy and Commerce Committee.
The Agriculture Committee requested executive comment from the USDA and EPA and referred the bill to its subcommittees on November 15, 1991.
Subcommittee hearings were held in November 1991 and again in March 1992, and an additional sponsor, Mr. Brown, was added in March 1992.
On May 19, 1992, a subcommittee held a mark-up session and forwarded the bill to the full Agriculture Committee with amendments.
No further action was recorded, and the bill never received a vote in either the committee or the full House before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pesticide registrants were better off: they avoided new periodic data requirements, review fees, the shifted burden of proof in EPA proceedings, and the negligible-risk tolerance standard and larger penalties the bill would have imposed.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a floor vote, so no roll-call record exists; its two sponsors were House Democrats, and the Democratic-controlled committees declined to advance it.

industries.note: The bill would require updated safety data every ten years, fees for registration reviews, cancellation authority over risky products, and criminal penalties up to $1,000,000 for knowing endangerment. The industry's cost of proving its products safe is the public's gain in safer food and fewer hazardous exposures.

Dealers would have to keep three years of sales records for restricted-use pesticides, and commercial applicators would face certification, supervised registration, five-year recertification, and training requirements. These are compliance burdens whose purpose is to prevent misuse that harms workers and the public.

Farmers would face new training and certification requirements for restricted-use pesticides and possible loss of some chemistry, but the bill also lets canceled pesticide stocks be sold off, lets minor-use registrations be delayed up to three years while alternatives are researched, and requires EPA to weigh effects on crop production and food prices before acting.

The bill sets a federal floor for pesticide residues that preempts stricter state limits unless EPA approves a waiver, which favors uniform national standards, while tighter negligible-risk tolerances and increased residue monitoring of imports and domestic food would raise compliance pressure. Consumers eat the residue limits either way.

The bill directs EPA to prioritize registration of ingredients significantly lower-risk than existing alternatives and requires annual reports on expediting biological pesticide registrations, opening market space for safer products.
